description: We’re computer science students at Toronto Metropolitan University who believe good health software should work anywhere, from a clinic in Toronto to a base on Mars.
summary:
Vitals Atlas is an accessible health dashboard that helps astronauts get timely medical help when support from Earth is limited. What makes prompt intervention even more difficult is that an astronaut may not realize they are experiencing a medical emergency or may be too unwell to call for help.

Vitals Atlas brings three capabilities together in one dashboard that works on a smartwatch, a tablet, or a laptop. Continuous health monitoring, informed by passive readings from wearables, allows for early problem identification. Coordinated emergency response orchestrates the crew’s actions by identifying who needs help, pinpointing their location, and assigning clear tasks so the team can act quickly and in sync. Proposed offline AI-assisted medical support runs on board and cites its sources. We designed every screen to ask less of people already carrying the weight of exhaustion, pain, or stress. Far from Earth, crews are their own first responders. Vitals Atlas equips them to act with confidence when a medical emergency strikes.
details:
How it works: Vitals Atlas runs on a smartwatch, a tablet or a laptop. A wearable such as the CSA’s Bio-Monitor smart shirt sends readings to the dashboard all the time. When an astronaut’s readings move outside her own usual range, the dashboard asks her one simple question, such as whether she has chest pain. If she answers Yes or Not sure, or doesn’t answer within 3 minutes, the crew doctor is alerted. The doctor sees the likely problem with its evidence and sources, then decides whether to monitor, confirm, dismiss or escalate. Escalating alerts the whole crew with who needs help, where she is and each person’s own task. Any crew member can send an SOS with a single press. A report goes to Earth automatically, but the crew starts care without waiting.

Proposed AI: An onboard medical AI model that needs no network. It would be trained on medical textbooks and peer-reviewed papers, say how sure it is and cite its sources. In our demo, its answers are scripted.

Data: Inspiration4 blood tests (NASA OSDR), DONKI solar storms, RadLab radiation doses, NASA-STD-3001 radiation limits, Human Research Program risks, and CSA Radi-N neutron readings and the ACTIS blood clot test.

Tools: JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, HTML and CSS.

Creativity: Each screen fits the person using it and the state they’re in. The patient gets one question with large buttons, the doctor gets the evidence, and responders get their task in the largest text. Silence counts as a signal, so help comes even when an astronaut can’t ask for it.

Factors we considered: accessibility (high-contrast text, large touch targets), undoable mistakes (a 10-second cancel for SOS and escalation), privacy (medical data shared only during an emergency), and medical responsibility (screening signals, not diagnoses, with the doctor making every decision).

Impact: Crews can handle medical emergencies far from Earth. The same approach could serve remote northern communities in Canada, where a doctor may be hours away.

Demo content is simulated. Vitals Atlas is not a medical device.
dataRefs: NASA OSD-569: Inspiration4 crew blood counts (hemoglobin, white cells)
NASA OSD-575: Inspiration4 crew metabolic panels (glucose, potassium, creatinine)
NASA DONKI: real solar storm records, replayed in the demo
NASA RadLab: measured radiation dose rates on Mars (Curiosity) and the ISS (DosTel)
projectRefs: CSA Radi-N2: neutron doses Canadian astronauts measured on the ISS, 2009–2019
CSA Bio-Monitor: the smart shirt in our design (no data used)
CSA ACTIS: the blood clot test the crew doctor can run in our design (mock result, no data used)
